113.title: Ash Wednesday: dust
113.hook: ashes on the forehead and the words: remember you are dust (Genesis 3:19)
113.howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday, Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and others go to church to receive a cross of ash on the forehead, with words recalling Genesis 3:19; Orthodox Christians begin Great Lent on Clean Monday instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epiphany: strangers from the east, a river, a wedding. Your line was the light is for everyone. Did an outsider show you something? Now the circle turns darker. Day one hundred thirteen.

One Wednesday in late winter or early spring, you might notice it on the train, at the office, in the grocery line. A dark smudge on someone's forehead. Sometimes it's a neat cross. Sometimes just a gray thumbprint. People who don't know lean over and say, hey, you've got something on your face. They know. They put it there on purpose, or rather, someone did, that morning or at lunch, in a church. A minister or priest dipped a thumb in ash, pressed it to their forehead, and said a few words from the third chapter of Genesis, words about dust. It's a reminder worn in public, for one day. Today's word is the day it happens.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE TRAIN.` → `YOU'VE GOT SOMETHING ON YOUR FACE.` → `ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Ash Wednesday. The first day of Lent. Often the ashes come from burning the palm branches of last year's Palm Sunday, so last year's celebration becomes this year's dust. And the words often echo what God says to Adam in Genesis. In the King James: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." That's blunt. Every life ends. In the Bible, ashes go with grief and turning around: Job, at the end of his long argument with God, says he repents "in dust and ashes." But here's the part that changes it. Go back one chapter in Genesis, to how the first human was made. "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." Readers of the Hebrew hear a pun here. The human is adam. The ground is adamah. An earthling, from the earth. So being dust isn't only bad news. It's what God picked up, and shaped, and breathed into. A psalm puts it tenderly: "he remembereth that we are dust." Not as a threat. As someone who knows how fragile you are. Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans and Methodists keep Ash Wednesday, and some other churches do too. Orthodox Christians don't; their Great Lent begins on a Monday called Clean Monday, after an evening when people ask one another's forgiveness. For Christians, the ash is a reminder in two directions: you are dust, and you are loved.
screen: `LAST YEAR'S PALMS, BURNED.` · `DUST THOU ART.` · `ADAM FROM ADAMAH.` · then, large: `HE REMEMBERETH THAT WE ARE DUST.` · then: `DUST, AND BREATHED INTO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch the ground. If there's a plant nearby, press a finger into its soil. If you're outside, touch the earth. If neither, look closely at the back of your hand. Settle, and breathe. Remember that you are made of the same stuff as the ground. You won't be here forever. Let that be true without panicking. Then notice your breath going in and out. If you pray, you can remember the other half: breathed into, and loved. If you don't, simply hold both at once: fragile, and here. The bell holds the time.
Ash Wednesday. The first day of Lent, when Christians in a number of churches receive ashes on the forehead and hear that they are dust. Today's word.
Your line: dust, and loved. Today, when you wash your face or your hands, remember both halves of it. Day one hundred thirteen.

what it means: dust, and loved. a reminder that you won't last forever, and that the dust is what God shaped and breathed into.

114.title: Lent: forty days
114.hook: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving, echoing Jesus in the desert
114.howItsDone: During Lent many Christians fast in some way, pray more and give to the poor; Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and abstain from meat on Fridays, Orthodox Christians traditionally fast from meat, dairy and eggs through Great Lent, and some Protestants give up or take up one personal practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash Wednesday, and your line: dust, and loved. Did you remember both halves when you washed your hands? The ash opens a season. Today, what comes next. Day one hundred fourteen.

Every spring you hear it at work, at school, in group chats. So what are you giving up for Lent? Chocolate. Coffee. Social media. Swearing. One person gives up nothing and says they're giving up giving things up. It can sound like a second round of New Year's resolutions. But the season started somewhere much older and much harder. In the Gospels, right after his baptism, Jesus goes out into the wilderness alone, and stays there. The King James says, "And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred." Hungry, alone, tested, in the desert. Today's word is the season Christians built around those forty days.
screen: `WHAT ARE YOU GIVING UP?` → `INTO THE WILDERNESS.` → `FORTY DAYS AND FORTY NIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Lent. The English name is usually traced to an old word for spring, the season when the days lengthen. In Greek and Latin the season is simply called the fortieth. Forty is a number the Bible keeps returning to. Forty days of rain for Noah. Forty days for Moses on the mountain. Forty years for Israel in the wilderness. Forty days for Elijah walking to the mountain of God. And forty days for Jesus in the desert. Readers hear forty as the Bible's number for a long, testing stretch that changes people. Lent is traditionally made of three practices, and they come from Jesus's own teaching in the Sermon on the Mount: prayer, fasting and giving to the poor. He doesn't say if you fast. He says when. Churches keep it differently. Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and abstain from meat on the Fridays of Lent. Orthodox Christians traditionally keep a fast without meat, dairy or eggs through Great Lent. Some Protestants choose something personal, or take something up instead: reading a Gospel, volunteering, calling someone each day. Some churches don't mark Lent at all. But a shared idea sits underneath. Giving something up isn't meant as a punishment. It's meant to make room. The hour you'd spend scrolling becomes an hour for prayer. The money you'd spend on coffee goes to someone who needs it. Some say the hunger itself becomes a reminder of what they're really hungry for. Less, so there's room. That's why Christians call it a season of preparation. It clears space for Easter.
screen: `LENCTEN: SPRING.` · `FORTY: THE BIBLE'S TESTING NUMBER.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, GIVING.` · `LESS, TO MAKE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one small Lenten thing. It doesn't have to be Lent right now. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself what's taking up too much room in your days. A habit, a screen, a snack, a complaint you keep repeating. Choose one small thing to set down for a week. Or choose one thing to take up in its place. Keep it small enough that you'll actually do it. If you pray, you can offer it to God. If you don't, just notice what fills the space. The bell holds the time.
Lent. Its English name is traced to an old word for spring. Forty days of prayer, fasting and giving before Easter, echoing Jesus in the desert. Today's word.
Your line: less, so there's room. Today, start your small thing, and when you feel its absence, let the gap remind you what you made room for. Day one hundred fourteen.

screen: `DAY 114 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PALM SUNDAY AND HOLY WEEK.`

115.title: Palm Sunday and Holy Week
115.hook: branches in, a cross by Friday; the week the whole year turns on
115.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday many churches bless and hand out palm branches, walk in procession and read the Passion; through Holy Week Christians gather for services each day toward Easter, and many walk the Stations of the Cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lent, forty days, and your line: less, so there's room. How is your small thing going? Lent walks toward one week. Today, we arrive at it. Day one hundred fifteen.

Jerusalem, a few days before Passover. The city is packed with Passover pilgrims, and Roman soldiers are watching the crowds. A man comes over the Mount of Olives riding a young donkey. Not a warhorse. A donkey. And the crowd goes wild. People pull off their cloaks and throw them on the road in front of him. Others cut branches from the trees. John's Gospel says they "Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord." It feels like a parade. It feels like the beginning of something. And by Friday of that same week, he'll be on a Roman cross. Today, the week that everything turns on.
screen: `PASSOVER, A PACKED CITY.` → `A DONKEY, NOT A WARHORSE.` → `BRANCHES AND CLOAKS ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Palm Sunday and Holy Week. Start with the shout. Hosanna. It sounds like a word of praise, and it became one, but it began as a plea. It comes from Hebrew in Psalm 118: save, please. Save us now. The crowd is shouting praise and a prayer for rescue at the same time. And the donkey matters. The prophet Zechariah had pictured Jerusalem's king coming humble, riding on a donkey. Jesus seems to choose that picture on purpose: a king, but not the kind with an army. Then the week unfolds. In the Gospels, Jesus clears the traders out of the temple. He teaches in its courts. A woman anoints him with costly perfume. On Thursday, a last supper with his friends. On Friday, the cross. On Saturday, silence. On Sunday, the empty tomb. People have long noticed how fast it turns, from palms to a cross in five days. Sometimes they say the same crowd that shouted hosanna shouted crucify, but the Gospels don't say that; they don't say who was in either crowd. Christians keep this week as the center of the whole year. On Palm Sunday, many churches hand out palm branches and walk in procession, then read the long story of Jesus's death, the Passion, so the whole week is felt at once. In Russia and other places where palms don't grow, Orthodox Christians carry pussy willow branches instead. In many places, people walk the Stations of the Cross, stopping to pray at fourteen scenes along the way to the cross. And in Jerusalem itself, pilgrims still walk down the Mount of Olives on Palm Sunday, waving branches, along roughly the road the donkey took.
screen: `HOSANNA: SAVE US, PLEASE.` · `A KING ON A DONKEY.` · `PALMS TO A CROSS IN FIVE DAYS.` · `THE CENTER OF THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk the road in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture a dusty road down a hill into a crowded city. Branches on the ground. The noise. A man on a donkey, moving slowly through all of it, toward whatever is coming. Walk beside him for a while. Notice what he might be feeling. If you pray, you can simply stay with him. If you don't, stay with the picture. Later today, walk one route slowly, to the store, around the block, down a hallway, and remember this road as you go. The bell holds the time.
Hosanna, a shout that began as a plea, from Hebrew save, please, and became both praise and a prayer for rescue.
Your line: the week everything turns. Today, walk one slow route, and let each step be a little remembering. Day one hundred fifteen.

116.title: Maundy Thursday
116.hook: from mandatum, commandment: love one another, and many churches wash feet
116.howItsDone: On Maundy Thursday churches in several traditions hold an evening service remembering the Last Supper, often with the washing of feet, and some end it by stripping the altar bare; some traditions practice foot washing at other times of the year as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Palm Sunday and Holy Week, hosanna, and your line: the week everything turns. Did you walk a slow route? Now we're at Thursday of that week, the last night. Day one hundred sixteen.

An upstairs room in Jerusalem. Evening. Supper is under way, and Jesus and his disciples are reclining at the table. Then the teacher stands up. He lays aside his outer robe, ties a towel around his waist, pours water into a basin, and starts washing his friends' feet, one by one. In that world, it was work for a servant, not a host. When he gets to Peter, Peter can't stand it. In the King James words: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." And Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." So Peter, being Peter, swings the other way and asks him to wash his hands and his head too. Today's word is the name of that night.
screen: `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM.` → `A TOWEL AND A BASIN.` → `THOU SHALT NEVER WASH MY FEET.`

segments.voice: Maundy. The name is usually traced to the Latin mandatum, which means commandment. It comes from what Jesus says later that night, in John's Gospel: "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another." In Latin, that sentence begins with mandatum, and it became the chant sung while feet were washed. So the name of the day is really: the day of the commandment. And the commandment has a picture attached. After he washes their feet, Jesus says: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." Love here isn't a feeling. It's a towel. It's kneeling. It's doing the job nobody wants. John tells the foot washing. Matthew, Mark and Luke tell what else happened that night: the Last Supper, when Jesus takes bread and wine and, in Luke and in Paul's letter, tells his friends to do this in remembrance of him. Christians understand that meal in different ways. Catholics and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood. Lutherans speak of Christ truly present in them; other Protestants of a spiritual presence, or a memorial. Churches that share communion trace it back to this night. And some churches still wash feet on Maundy Thursday. Popes have knelt to wash the feet of prisoners and refugees. In some churches, everyone takes a turn washing someone else's. In Britain, the monarch hands out special coins, Maundy money, to older people each year, a faint echo of the old custom. Then, in some churches, the altar is stripped bare. The night ends in a garden, with an arrest.
screen: `MANDATUM: COMMANDMENT.` · `LOVE ONE ANOTHER, AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.` · `LOVE IS A TOWEL.` · `A SUPPER, A BASIN, A BARE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the towel. Settle, and breathe. Bring back the room, the basin, the teacher with the towel. Then think of your own home, or work. What's the job nobody wants? The dishes in the sink. The trash. The shared bathroom. The email nobody answers. Pick one. Decide that today, you'll do it for someone else, without mentioning it. If you pray, you can offer it as a way of keeping the commandment. If you don't, just notice what it's like to serve quietly. The bell holds the time.
Maundy. From the Latin mandatum, commandment: love one another. The Thursday before Easter, when some churches wash feet. Today's word.
Your line: love one another. Today, wash someone's dishes, or do their least favorite job, and don't say a word about it. Day one hundred sixteen.

117.title: Good Friday
117.hook: churches strip altars, keep silence, and venerate the cross
117.howItsDone: On Good Friday churches are left bare and some Christians fast and keep silence; Catholics venerate the cross at an afternoon service without Mass, Orthodox Christians carry the epitaphios, an icon of Christ's burial, in procession, and some Protestants keep services from noon to three.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maundy Thursday: a towel, a basin, and your line: love one another. Did you do someone's least favorite job? That night ended in a garden, with an arrest. Today is the next day. Day one hundred seventeen.

On Good Friday, a church can look robbed. The altar is bare wood or stone. No flowers. No candles burning. The cloths are gone. Often the bells stay silent. People come in without talking, and sit. Some services start at noon and run until three in the afternoon. Matthew writes: "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour." By the old way of counting the day, that's noon to three. So some Christians keep those hours, in silence, or with long readings, or with a single hymn. Today's word is the day's strange name.
screen: `A CHURCH THAT LOOKS ROBBED.` → `NO CANDLES, NO BELLS.` → `NOON TO THREE.`

segments.voice: Good Friday. First, what the Gospels say happened. After his arrest, Jesus is questioned by the high priest's council and then handed to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate sentences him, and Roman soldiers crucify him outside the city wall. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment, used for rebels and slaves, meant to be slow and public. His friends mostly scatter. Women who had followed him from Galilee stay, watching. And in John's Gospel, his last words are three in English: "It is finished." In Greek, it's a single word, tetelestai. It doesn't mean it's over, I give up. It means it's complete. Done. Accomplished. Christians hear it as the end of a work, not a defeat. So why call the day good? Honestly, nobody is sure. Good may be the old English sense of holy. Some suggest it came from God's Friday. The sources don't settle it. But Christians call it good because they believe something was done that day for the whole world, out of love. They explain how in more than one way. Churches keep the day differently. Catholics celebrate no Mass; in the afternoon they read the Passion, and people come forward one by one to kneel before the cross, touch it, or kiss it. Orthodox Christians carry a cloth icon of Christ's burial in procession, and lay it in a tomb decked with flowers. Some Protestants gather for three hours at noon, or for a service where candles are put out one by one, until the church is dark.
screen: `PILATE, SOLDIERS, A ROMAN CROSS.` · `TETELESTAI: IT IS COMPLETE.` · `WHY GOOD? NOBODY IS SURE.` · `THE CROSS, THE TOMB, THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep silence. Settle, and breathe. For the next two minutes, don't fill the quiet. No music, no plans, no words. If you have a cross, you can look at it. If you pray, you can simply stay near it, the way the women stayed. If you don't, let the silence be for anyone who is suffering today. Later, at noon, or whenever you can, keep three more minutes of silence. Set an alarm if you need to. The bell holds the time.
Good Friday. The day Christians remember Jesus's death on the cross, with bare altars, silence and the veneration of the cross. Today's word.
Your line: it is finished. Today, keep three minutes of silence at noon. And finish one thing you've left undone. Day one hundred seventeen.

118.title: Holy Saturday
118.hook: the quiet day; in the old vigil a new fire is lit in the dark
118.howItsDone: On Holy Saturday churches stay bare and quiet during the day; after dark churches in several traditions hold the Easter Vigil, lighting a new fire and the Easter candle and passing its flame from person to person, and Orthodox churches pass the light at midnight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Good Friday: a Roman cross, and your line: it is finished. Did you keep three minutes of silence? Today is the day in between. Day one hundred eighteen.

The day after a funeral has its own kind of quiet. The flowers are still there. The casseroles are in the fridge. Everyone has gone home. Nothing is happening. The Gospels give this day almost nothing. Jesus has been laid in a new tomb cut in the rock, and a great stone rolled to the door. Luke says the women went home, prepared spices to anoint the body, "and rested the sabbath day according to the commandment." Matthew adds only that a guard is posted and the stone sealed. Beyond that, the text is quiet. Nobody in the story knows what comes next. Today's word is the name of that silence.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER THE FUNERAL.` → `A STONE ACROSS THE DOOR.` → `THEY RESTED THE SABBATH.`

segments.voice: Holy Saturday. For most of the day, churches stay bare and quiet. No celebration yet. It's a day for waiting in grief. But Christians have also wondered where Jesus was that day. The Apostles' Creed says, in the Book of Common Prayer, "He descended into hell." And the First Letter of Peter says he "went and preached unto the spirits in prison." Out of those lines grew an old picture, sometimes called the harrowing of hell. In the Orthodox Easter icon, Christ stands on the broken gates of death, pulling Adam and Eve up out of their tombs by the wrists. Christians read that line of the creed in more than one way, some as a descent to the dead, some as a way of saying he truly died. Then night falls, and something happens in the dark. In the old Easter Vigil, kept by Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans and others, the people gather outside, or at the back of a dark church, and a new fire is lit. From it, one tall candle is lit, the Easter candle. It's carried in slowly, and someone sings: the light of Christ. People light small candles from it, then from each other, until the whole dark church is glowing. In Orthodox churches, it happens near midnight. Every light goes out. The priest comes out holding a single flame and invites everyone to come and receive the light, and it passes from candle to candle through the crowd, out into the street. John's Gospel has a line for it: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not."
screen: `A DAY OF SILENCE AND WAITING.` · `HE DESCENDED INTO HELL.` · `A NEW FIRE IN THE DARK.` · `CANDLE TO CANDLE, INTO THE STREET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in the dark, then light one light. If you can, turn off the lights around you, or close your eyes. Settle, and breathe. Let the dark be dark for a while. Notice what it's like not to know what comes next. Don't rush it. Then, near the end, turn on one small light, or light a candle if it's safe, or simply open your eyes. Watch how much one flame changes a room. If you pray, you can welcome it as a sign of what Christians wait for. If you don't, just notice the difference. The bell holds the time.
Holy Saturday. The quiet day between the cross and Easter, which ends in the dark with a new fire. Today's word.
Your line: light in the dark. Today, notice where one small light could change a dark room for someone, and be that light if you can. Day one hundred eighteen.

119.title: Easter is fifty days
119.hook: Christ is risen! He is risen indeed! Orthodox Pascha often falls on a later date, by the old calendar
119.howItsDone: Christians celebrate Easter, or Pascha, with services at dawn, at the vigil or at midnight, greeting one another with Christ is risen and the reply He is risen indeed; many churches keep the Easter season for fifty days, to Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holy Saturday, and your line: light in the dark. This week walked a hard road: ashes, Lent, palms, a towel, a cross, a silent tomb. Seventeen weeks on the path. Today, the stone moves. Day one hundred nineteen.

Midnight, outside an Orthodox church. Hundreds of people holding candles in the street, some of them kids who are way past bedtime. The priest steps out and calls, Christ is risen! In a Greek church, Christos anesti. And the whole crowd shouts back: Truly he is risen! He says it again, and again, louder. Then there are fireworks, bells, and people kissing each other three times on the cheek. For weeks afterward, friends greet each other that way on the street and even in text messages. In English-speaking churches you'll hear it as: Christ is risen! He is risen indeed! It all goes back to a Sunday morning, and some women at an empty tomb, where an angel says, "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said." Today's word is the feast's name in Greek and Latin.

segments.voice: Pascha. It's the Greek and Latin name for Easter, and it comes from the Hebrew Pesach, Passover. Jesus died and rose at Passover time, and the first Christians, who were Jewish, heard his death and rising as a new passing over, from death to life. Paul writes, in the King James words: "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us." So in French, Easter is Pâques; in Spanish, Pascua. English says Easter, a word whose origin is still debated. The English reply echoes Luke. When two disciples rush back to Jerusalem, the others meet them with the news: "The Lord is risen indeed." Now, the date. Western churches keep Easter on the Sunday after the first full moon of spring, by their reckoning. Orthodox churches count by the older Julian calendar, so Orthodox Pascha often falls later, sometimes by weeks, and some years both land on the same day. Families with a foot in both traditions sometimes celebrate twice. And Easter isn't only a day. Like Christmas, it's a season, and a longer one. Fifty days, all the way to Pentecost. Churches keep the candles burning and the alleluias going. For Christians, this is the center of everything. Paul put it bluntly: "And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." That's the weight behind the shout, kept up for fifty days: he is risen indeed.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry good news. Settle, and breathe. Think of the women running from the tomb, scared and overjoyed at the same time, with news they could barely say. Now think of one piece of good news in your own life, or someone else's, that deserves to be told. A recovery. A new job. A kindness someone doesn't know about. Picture the person who should hear it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it first. If you don't, just hold it for a moment. Then plan to tell them today. The bell holds the time.
